assessmentSettings.feedbackPolicy: Show concise learning feedback after submission; keep full answer keys in the teacher setup file.

requiredUploads: relativity-timekeeping-evidence.png — at least four trials including a fast and a slow clock
requiredCopiedValues: Students type short values read from the on-screen tables; the assessment template blocks clipboard actions.

humanReviewTriggers: Student response conflicts with the uploaded evidence image.
Student reports values that fall outside the expected range but the evidence image may support them.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student uses valid alternative vocabulary or reasoning not covered by the model answer.
Student answer is blank, copied from the prompt, or too vague to verify.
Student cites no data when the prompt requires their own recorded values.

questions.prompt: Report one trial from your data table where the clock ended up fast and one where it ended up slow. For each, give the altitude, the speed, the GR value, the SR value, and the net drift. Then explain what changed between the two trials to flip the sign.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on reporting all five values for both of your own trials and explaining what changed between them to flip the sign of the net drift.

criteria: Reports both trials with all five values from the student's own table.

Identifies that the fast clock sits at high altitude where the gravity term is large and the orbital speed is low, while the slow clock sits at low altitude where the gravity term is small and the orbital speed is high.
And states that the sign of the net drift is set by which of the two competing terms is larger.
Reports both trials with some values and states which effect dominates, but does not connect altitude and speed to the size of each term.
Reports no data from the table, or claims only one of the two effects is present.

commonMisconceptions: Treats only one of the two effects as present.
Thinks altitude always wins regardless of orbit.
Reports the net drift without the GR and SR values that produce it.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your answer uses your own recorded data and connects it to the correct physics idea.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by adding the specific values you recorded and naming the physics concept that explains them.
feedback.noCredit: Return to your evidence image, identify the values this question asks about, and explain them using the target concept.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the reasoning is unusual but could be correct, or if the cited values disagree with the uploaded evidence.

questions.prompt: Choose one of the non-GPS cases from the evidence cards - the cosmic-ray muons, the Pound-Rebka tower, Sirius B, the storage-ring muons, or the optical clocks. Describe what that experiment measured and explain which of the two effects it confirms, and why it counts as independent evidence for what you measured in this lab.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on naming a specific case, assigning it to the correct effect, and explaining why it counts as independent evidence rather than a repeat of the GPS test.

criteria: Names a specific case and what was measured.
Correctly assigns it to the motion effect (muons, storage ring) or the gravity effect (Pound-Rebka, Sirius B, optical clocks).

And explains that because the experiment uses a different system and a different measurement technique from a satellite clock, agreement with the same theory is independent confirmation rather than a repeat of the same test.
Describes a case and assigns the correct effect, but does not explain why it is independent evidence.
Assigns the wrong effect, describes no measurement, or restates the GPS case.

commonMisconceptions: Assigns a gravitational test to the motion effect or the reverse.
Describes a case without saying what was measured.
Restates the GPS result instead of choosing an independent case.
